utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon to those in court. The -- yesterday there were two objections made by counsel for the Defence, and I wonder whether it would be convenient at this point, Mr. Weiner, for that to be dealt with by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That would be fine. Would I still be allowed to remain seated through the day, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You may accept that to be the position unless we get ill of sorts and countermand that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, the Defence raised two issues yesterday. I'd like to address the first one. They stated, it's indicated in the indictment, that the Prosecution, and I'm now quoting, was "trying to extend the time period in the indictment." They further stated that we were "extending the indictment to contain omissions and events that are not contained in the indictment"; and the third matter was that we were bringing charges against the accused outside that specific time period -- no: "that charges against the accused outside that specific time period should be excluded or their importance should be minimal." And those are three quotes from yesterday's transcript. First, we are not charging the accused with any activity outside of the normal indictment period. Acts that are occurring prior to December 6th are an integral part of the Prosecution's case and are mentioned throughout the indictment. In count 6 of the indictment, there is discussion of the independence of Croatia on or about October 8th. In count 11 there is discussion of the attack that was launched against Dubrovnik beginning on October 1st. In count 12, they have the history of the JNA's attack, the one which began on October 1st. In count 13 there is discussion of the shelling attacks on the Old Town from 23 October to 6 December. In count 22 there's discussion of shelling attacks on the Old Town from 23 October to 6th December and that the Old Town was a UNESCO protected site. In counts 29 and 30 of the indictment there is discussion as to the extent of the damage. Thus we are not referring to matters outside of the indictment. In addition to that, the accused is being charged with liability pursuant to Articles 7(1) and 7(3). As the Court knows, 7(3) requires that a superior, or a commander have knowledge or have reason to know of the acts of his subordinates and that he failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent these acts. The evidence that we wish to tender relates to this issue. From the prior acts, the accused Strugar had reason to know of the vulnerability of the Old Town, that even with standing orders from the highest levels of the Yugoslav government not to attack the Old Town, the Old Town was still shelled in October and shelled in November. The defendant's, or the accused's, failure to take reasonable precautions or punish those who acted resulted in the unlawful attack which occurred on December 6th. There is case law which supports our position that the evidence of prior acts is admissible. In the Vasiljevic case, the trial judgement dated 29 November 2002, it concerns two incidents which occurred in which a number of persons were murdered. In paragraph 46, which appears on page 18, they talk about the knowledge of the defendant -- I'm sorry, of the accused. And they first talk about these acts which were placed, which were introduced by the Commonwealth prior to the dates of the actual indictment period, and it says: "A particularly violent and feared group of paramilitaries, Serb paramilitaries, was led by the co-accused Milan Lukic. In the course of a few weeks, this group committed many crimes ranging from looting to murders." And then three sentences later, it says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm very sorry. Three sentences later, it says: "Despite that knowledge, the accused was seen together with these men on several occasions during the period relevant to the indictment." So they are talking about the defendant's knowledge based on acts which were introduced prior to the period which the allegations concern. Later, in another case, in the case of Prosecutor versus Kvocka, the trial judgement is 2 November 2001. In paragraph 318, and I'll read you part of it, which is on page 90: "Information that would make a superior suspicious that crimes might be committed includes past behaviour of subordinates or a history of mistreatment. For instance, a military commander who has received information that some of the soldiers under his command have a violent or unstable character or have been drinking prior to being sent on mission may be considered as having the required knowledge. Similarly, if a superior has prior knowledge that women detained by male guards in detention facilities are likely to be subjected to sexual violence, that would put him on sufficient notice that extra measures are demanded in order to prevent such crimes." That is the same theory that we're proceeding on here. And further, in the -- sorry. One second. In the Prosecutor versus Kupreskic appeal judgement, dated 23 October 2001, they also dealt with prior uncharged crimes, and the Court, in allowing that evidence to be used as corroborative evidence and to prove different issues, stated: "Courts --" they referred to how other countries deal with evidence of prior crimes or acts, and that could be prior or subsequent, and stated that: "Courts in England and Wales, Australia and the United States admit evidence of crimes or wrongful acts committed by the defendant other than those charged in the indictment if the other crimes are introduced to demonstrate a special knowledge, opportunity, or identification of the defendant that would make it more likely that he committed the instant crime as well." The case law in this Tribunal has allowed the use of prior and subsequent bad acts. Finally, I would just like to point the Chamber's attention to Rule 89(C), which states that a Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value. As we stated, this evidence constitutes an integral part of our case, was mentioned in our pre-trial brief in several sections, in several sections of the indictment. It is probative, it's highly relevant, and it should be admitted into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner. Does it perhaps, at bottom, come down to this; that the physical acts that are the subject of the charges relate to the 6th of December but that you are bringing your case in part against the accused on the basis of his command responsibility and his knowledge and anticipation of what forces under his command might do; and in that regard, his mental state, that is, what he anticipated or should have anticipated about the conduct of the forces under his command on the 6th of December would be relevantly informed by conduct which occurred at dates earlier than the 6th of December and could also be informed by conduct that occurred later?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. That is our view, Your Honour, said much more eloquently and succinctly than I did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Although, I heard you first.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. We would like to use the prior and subsequent acts to prove his knowledge, mental state at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If would you like to add something, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to respond very briefly to my learned friend. I am very glad that he mentioned the cases that were tried before this Tribunal before; Vasiljevic, Kvocka, and Kupreskic. I would like to recall very briefly certain relevant aspects of these cases, starting with the Kvocka and Vasiljevic cases. The first important difference and the first important reason why the rationale underlying these cases cannot apply to our case is that in neither of the aforementioned cases - Kvocka, Vasiljevic and others - were not charged with command responsibility. They were charged under Article 7(3), but the judgement did not find them guilty under Article 7(3). That is the first important difference. The second important difference has to do with what I mentioned yesterday, and that is the time of the indictment. The time of the indictment in Kvocka and the others is from the 30th of April, 1992 to the 31st of August, 1992. The prior conduct of soldiers, guards, et cetera, from which the commanding officer could have perhaps drawn conclusions falls within the time of the indictment. For instance, abuse of a prisoner by a drunken guard happened at the time covered by the indictment, from the 30th of April to the 31st of August, 1992. Therefore, their situation does not apply to our case. Our period begins with the 31st of December. This other conduct does not apply. In Kvocka and Vasiljevic, it is the same case. All prior conduct in their cases falls within the time of the indictment. If in the judgement of the Trial Chamber in Kvocka and Vasiljevic cases guilt has been found, it is certainly in relation to the conduct of subordinates at the time covered by the indictment, which is not our case. In our case, we have the 6th of December as the date of commencement of the alleged crime, which is prosecution -- persecution - sorry - and in their cases the alleged crime falls within the period of the entire existence of the Omarska camp, in which certain conduct took place. So the jurisprudence of this Tribunal does not point in the direction quoted by my learned friend, and that is the essence of the remarks we voiced yesterday; namely, the claim that the 6th of December is a result or an outcome of something that happened prior to that is untenable. The Prosecutor, if I try to explain it briefly, is trying to say that the premises for the events of the 6th of December were created outside of the indicted period. That is not allowed before our Tribunal. It is not allowed to extend the period through the back door. This is too important an issue for me to leave without remarks. It is perhaps more fitting for me to put my remarks in writing and address a motion to the Trial Chamber because it seems likely that this will be a key issue in our case on which many things will be decided, namely what happened before and what happened after the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do I understand from your comments, Mr. Petrovic, that you would propose to bring a formal written motion with supporting submissions in writing on this point to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I only wish to suggest and point out the importance of this issue. As to the need for a written submission, I would follow your instructions. Therefore, if the Trial Chamber believes that it is necessary - and I think it is necessary - and if you share the opinion of the Defence, so General Strugar, then of course we would be prepared to treat the issue in writing and present you with a submission. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We share your view, Mr. Petrovic, of the fundamental importance of this issue to the conduct of this hearing. We would, therefore, encourage you to bring your submissions forward in writing so that you will have had an opportunity to consider them carefully when you prepare them so that the Office of the Prosecutor will have an opportunity to consider them in what we would propose should be a written response, and we will then ourselves be able to look at this matter thoroughly, because exactly as you say, the decision on this issue will affect a great deal about the conduct of the hearing and the issues to be considered, so that we would value your carefully prepared written submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I have from you an indication of when you believe you would be able to bring those forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe it could be sometime in the beginning of January; in the first week of our sittings in January we would be able to file our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What I would propose is that when those submissions have been received -- you might need seven days, do you think, Mr. Weiner, to respond, or is that being too ambitious for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. We'll get it done as soon as possible. When they file their motion in limine, we will respond to it. Seven days is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And we will then take the matter formally under our consideration and deliver a decision so that that will guide the parties through the balance of the hearing. Thank you for that. Also raised yesterday, if I remember correctly, was the question of the film that was shown. Do you wish to put any submissions about that in response, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. They just raised a few questions. I'm not that certain what the objection is, but with regard to who the producer is, if you look at the credits at the end, it's the Institute for the Restoration of Dubrovnik, and the producer is Orlando Films from Dubrovnik. We were hoping to tender the film with some witness in the future. At that point, we could accept whatever objections or we could meet with counsel, maybe ahead of time, probably to save time here and see if we can resolve what issues that they're not pleased with. Maybe we can come to some agreement on the film. Whatever they please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me, I would like only briefly to recall our objection of yesterday in two sentences. In the hitherto practice of this Tribunal, as far as our Defence team knows, during opening statements, even if there is a film to present to the Trial Chamber, it can only be a film resulting from the work of associates of the OTP or the OTP itself. It is highly unusual for the Trial Chamber to present -- to be presented with, during opening Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. statements, with a film that was made for propaganda purposes by an institution completely outside of this Tribunal. As far as we know, this is simply not part of the Tribunal practice. The opening statement is a work product of the OTP, not anyone outside it. That is my first point. My second point is related to the first one. Namely, in the film we saw yesterday, certain qualifications are made that are inconsistent with the contents of the indictment. The armed conflict, which is the subject of our interest in this case, is qualified as "the war for the defence of Croatia" or "the homeland war" or something else. If it is the position of the Prosecution that it was a homeland war and not an armed conflict, as stated in the indictment, that considerably changes the parameters of our hearings. It changes the qualification of events that are the subject of our interest. This needs to be clarified. Is the Prosecution holding the position that we are discussing here the homeland war and the defence of Croatia or we are discussing an armed conflict involving a third party in the role of aggressor, as is usually claimed for propaganda purposes? That is our point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you assist us on that point, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: With regard to the first point, I'm not aware of any rule that indicates that films or photographs can only be produced if they are -- if they were made or taken by the Office of the Prosecutor. In other cases, films have been used. I believe in the Krstic case they utilised a film in closing argument from the JNA. It was some sort of publicity film of General Mladic. There is no requirements that I'm aware of, and I am not aware of any case where requirements have been set as to the use of film. With regard to opening statements, though, an opening statement is nothing more than a road map explaining what the Prosecutor's upcoming case will be. An opening statement is not evidence. An opening statement is simply a statement to the Court and to the Defence and to the public exactly what the Prosecutor plans to introduce. The use of films, photographs, documents, maps, plats are commonly used in jurisdictions throughout the world. There is no requirement that only films or documents or photographs made by one party may be introduced. Once again, if they would also like to file a motion in limine opposing the introduction of that film or if they would like to sit and meet with us and discuss the matter with us outside of the courtroom, tell us what objections they have, maybe we can come to some agreement in relation to its admission; that's fine. But at this point, unless we're viewing this as a motion in limine, I'm not really certain how they would like us to respond. It's nothing more than a statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I, for my part, I have not seen this to be anything of a formal motion but one essentially in which counsel for the Defence, quite reasonably, perhaps, ask is it the content of the film which is the case you are making about the nature of the armed conflict or is it some of the things that you yourself said earlier? Because there is a difference that has been identified between the two. Now, are you relying on the content of the film as demonstrating the nature of the armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. Witnesses will testify as to the nature of the armed conflict. The film is a view of the area of Dubrovnik from all different angles. It's also -- we also have portions of the film which show December 6th, and it shows the bombing which occurred during that period. Also, the extent of the damage and the restoration work. That is what the nature of the film is; basically scenes to be observed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I think it is made clear then that those representing Mr. Strugar can accept that you are not relying on what is said in the film as going to the nature of the armed conflict with which we are concerned. As to the balance of the matter, the question of whether or not the film is properly admissible and will be admitted into evidence are questions that will arise should you reach a point in your case when you want to introduce that film into evidence, and I think probably at that point, if Mr. Petrovic still has concerns, he would be able then to object to that film coming into evidence and we can look at that question then. I would, though, suggest, Mr. Petrovic, that it has been indicated that Mr. Weiner would be ready and willing to talk to you about the film, and I think it would be useful if that were followed up between you and you did discuss the film. It may be that any difficulties you have can be resolved between you before the point is reached later in the case when it seems Mr. Weiner will try to formally introduce the film into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, your conclusion and the statement of Mr. Weiner is satisfactory to us as it was phrased, and we consider this clarified. As for the admissibility of the film itself, we will certainly follow your advice and discuss this with our learned friends when the time comes in order to try to minimise the number of problems we bring to your attention to make our work as expedient as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Petrovic and Mr. Weiner. Well, I think we reach a point where we might hear your first witness then, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you'd allow me just two minutes. The Defence of General Strugar does not wish to go again into the issue of the submission regarding the health examination of our client, and we do not want to preempt your decision. We are expecting and hope that it will be favourable to our submission. And without anticipating either your decision or the outcome of the health examination, allow me to ask you to put some time limits on our work for the couple of following days. General Strugar has been complaining to us both yesterday and the day before yesterday that the time he had to spend here was a great strain on him. So I should like to ask, if I may, very kindly to limit the time he has to spend here for the next couple of days to two hours. Another thing I would like to bring to your notice is that General Strugar arrived in the building of the Tribunal today already at 12.30, which is close to two hours before the sitting began, which makes things more difficult for him, and that is another reason why we should like the Trial Chamber to consider the issue, with the assistance of all the supporting services, and see if it is possible to arrange things in such a way as to minimise the time General Strugar has to spend in transportation and waiting. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have given some preliminary consideration to the hours that we will sit during the balance of this week, especially because of the concerns that you, Mr. Rodic and Mr. Petrovic, have expressed about the present general health of your client, and what we will attempt to do this afternoon is to have just one break and then conclude the hearing sometime between 5.30 and 6.00, rather than sitting on until 7.00. That way may make the afternoons more manageable for your client and, I understand, will not present any great inconvenience to your own situation, Mr. Weiner, or that of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. We would agree to any limitation of the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I won't fix an exact time at the moment. It will just depend at what point the witness may be in evidence, but we will aim to finish at a convenient time between 5.30 and 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your understanding, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If the witness could take the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you would be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Examined by Mr. Weiner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Would you state your name, please.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Adrien Paul Stringer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us where you live.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: In Haslemere, near London.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Sixty-seven.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you employed at this time?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your status?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm retired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you last employed, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I was employed by the Ministry of Defence in London.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you -- just before you retired, what position did you serve in?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I was Director of Security for the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you work for the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Since 1962, retiring in 1995, at the end of 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at the end of your tenure with the Ministry of Defence, you said you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the end of your tenure with the Ministry of Defence, you indicated you severed as Director of Security. Could you tell us what your responsibilities were.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. They were responsibilities in respect of physical and personnel security, personnel security for the civilian employees in the Ministry of Defence and the physical security in respect of their buildings and premises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you hold that position?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Four years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, prior to that, did you ever serve in the military, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you serve?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I served two years national service, followed by about 13 years in the territorial army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "the territorial army," could that be characterised as the reserves?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, it could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what position did you retire as from the reserves?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: As a major.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, what we're going to do is slow down a bit because they have to translate each of our answers into Bosnian/Serbian/Croatian. So let us move to September of 1991. Could you tell us where you were.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I was in London, working at the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you receive some request?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I was asked if I would be prepared to join the European Community Monitoring Mission in the former -- in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you were asked, how did you respond?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I agreed to take up this post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive some sort of briefing while in London?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I had a short briefing, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who gave you this briefing?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Basically, the Defence intelligence staffs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they tell you at this briefing?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: The general situation pertaining in Croatia and Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you shown any photographs or maps?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: We were shown maps, not photographs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you where you would be heading?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you in fact go to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you arrive?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: On the 5th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you briefed when you arrived, when you arrived in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: By the ambassador who was in charge of the mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you assigned?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I was assigned initially to the tasking cell of the mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell the Chamber, what is a tasking cell?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: A tasking cell is that part of the mission which deals with operational matters and prepares reports for onward transmission to the Presidency at The Hague at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are they also involved in assignments?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: They do. They assign individuals to various mission activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people serve in a tasking cell?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: In the tasking cell, there are normally four people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you initially assigned?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, in the cell itself. The duties of the officials in the cell were interchangeable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you serve in the tasking cell?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Initially for one week. This was the normal period for serving in that cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after serving one week, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I was then assigned to one of the mobile missions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as part of that, what was your -- what were your responsibilities? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: They were varied, but essentially it was going round Zagreb itself to visit the Yugoslavian army, the JNA, who were in their barracks within and around Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you visiting the JNA troops in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: We were visiting the JNA troops because they were confined within those barracks by the Croatian forces that had surrounded them, and we needed to satisfy ourselves that they were being reasonably looked after within the confines of their barracks. And also, of course, that they were not going to try and attack and break out of those barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often did you visit the JNA troops?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: On a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often did you perform -- I'm sorry. How long did you perform this function?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I performed it for about a couple of weeks. A couple of weeks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your next assignment?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Next assignment was to go to the town of Osijek where there had been hostilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were you -- what was your purpose in going there?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: The purpose of going to Osijek was to establish a liaison with the JNA forces that were facing Osijek at the time, but we were unable to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your next assignment, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: The next assignment was to go to Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever heard of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I had indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I was not familiar with the city itself, but I had read all about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What had you learned from your readings?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: That it was a city in Yugoslavia, in Croatia, that was of historical importance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your reading include any information about its economic value?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: We believe that its economic value was extremely high in respect of Croatia, because it was Croatia's main tourist attraction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, prior to going to Dubrovnik, did you receive any briefings?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: We did receive briefings from within the tasking cell, because a team had been sent to Dubrovnik -- do you want me to go on?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: A team had been sent into Dubrovnik prior to my going there because there had been attacks around Dubrovnik at the time, and we were very concerned that there might be an escalation of hostilities in the area, and in particular against the old city of Dubrovnik itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What had they told you when you were briefed in Zagreb about Dubrovnik, about those attacks or the situation as it existed?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: The situation as it existed was that Dubrovnik was in fact blockaded so that supplies could not get through, that the water and electricity was cut off partly by hostile activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your purpose in going to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: The purpose in going to Dubrovnik was to attempt to facilitate a dialogue between the Croatian authorities in Dubrovnik and the JNA forces that were in the area and causing hostilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you who you would be meeting?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did they say you would be meeting with in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Arrangements had been made by the team that we were relieving for us to meet General Ruzinovski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you to meet with General Ruzinovski?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Because it was understood that he was in command of the JNA forces in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you what unit or group he commanded?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: This was the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who else did they tell you he would be meeting, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I had no specific names other than the general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regard to the Croatian officials, did they give you any information as to who you would be meeting?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: They told us that we would be meeting with the Crisis Committee of the Dubrovnik community which comprised the mayor, the president of the assembly, and several other officials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you why they wanted you to meet with the Crisis Committee and General Ruzinovski, why those persons?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Because they were the people who were primarily involved on the Croatian side. The Crisis Committee was managing effectively the affairs of Dubrovnik, whilst on the JNA side General Ruzinovski was in charge of the forces surrounding Dubrovnik at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when they told you about this upcoming meeting, did they tell you what sort of issues they wanted you to discuss with the two sides?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. The Crisis Committee were particularly concerned about the blockade of Dubrovnik and the restoration of the utilities, i.e., water and electricity to the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the names of any other JNA official mentioned that you should be meeting?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Not at that stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you leave for Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you leave?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I left on the 10th -- I believe it was the 10th of October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you get there?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: We drove by car to Rijeka, where we boarded a ferry called the Slavija, and went by ferry to Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you drive directly from Rijeka to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Because it was considered too dangerous at that time to proceed over land.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was it too dangerous?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Because there had been hostilities in the intervening area between Zagreb and Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you took the ferry to Dubrovnik, was your trip interrupted at any time?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. We were stopped by a JNA naval vessel that wished to confirm our bona fides and whether we had on board any unauthorised personnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they allow you to pass?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you arrive in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: We arrived in Dubrovnik at about half past 6.00 that evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what date?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: The 10th of October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after you arrived, did you meet with anyone?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: We met with the previous team, who again briefed us on the situation pertaining in Dubrovnik and confirming that arrangements had been made for us to meet General Ruzinovski and his staff in Montenegro the following day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, where did this meeting or briefing take place?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: On board the Slavija. It was a quick turnaround.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "the Slavija," that's the ferry?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Sorry. The ferry, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive a briefing -- more of an extensive briefing from this team?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Not terribly extensive, no more than we had already been made aware of in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you who the commander of the JNA forces in the area was?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, General Ruzinovski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you shown any maps or photographs?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Not photographs. We had maps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did they show you on the maps?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: The general area of the JNA forces and the front line as it related to Dubrovnik and Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next day, October 11th. Could you tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. On October the 11th, the following day, the team, including myself, went by motor vessel to the Bay of Kotor, and we were escorted into -- I think it was -- I can't remember the name, actually. Anyway, it was the port on the Bay of Kotor, where we were escorted to the JNA headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was in Montenegro, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: In Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the name Zelenika --

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Zelenika is the place, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who was present with you?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: On our side?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, with the ECMM team.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: With the ECMM, myself; Mr. Zak, a Polish gentleman; and a Mr. Nolan, an Irish gentleman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now when, we say "ECMM," for the record, could you tell us what we're referring to.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, it's the European Economic Community's Monitoring Mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, once you departed the boat, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: We went to -- we were escorted to what we understood to be the military hospital there, where we were taken to a conference room to meet the general and his staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was with the general?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: On the JNA side, there was Vice-Admiral Jokic, a Captain Svicevic - excuse me if I must pronounce the names - and a Captain Jeremic Sofronije.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And including General Ruzinovski?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Including General Ruzinovski, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you had this meeting, were you seated or were you standing?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: No. We were seated at a large conference table.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you describe the seating arrangement to the Court.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: On the JNA side, General Ruzinovski sat in the middle, and he was flanked by the admiral, the captain, and the other -- the two captains, Captain Sofronije.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was on the other side of the table?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: On the other side of the table was myself in the middle, flanked by Mr. Nolan and Mr. Zak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did someone run or lead the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: General Ruzinovski ran the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who spoke on the JNA side?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: General Ruzinovski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone else speak?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who spoke on the European Monitor side?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the meeting begin?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: The meeting began with introductions, with General Ruzinovski outlining the area of his command, which I believe ran from the Bay of Kotor to Mostar and to Slano.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if that area includes the city of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he tell you what his position was?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Commander of the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the purpose of this meeting, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: The purpose of the meeting was to obtain agreement for the JNA authorities and the Dubrovnik authorities to get together and also to secure some agreement concerning the cease-fire around Dubrovnik and the lifting of the blockades of Dubrovnik and the repair to the electricity and water supplies of the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you discussed these issues, what happened?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: After we discussed these issues, General Ruzinovski appointed a liaison officer for us, which was Captain Jeremic Sofronije. He also advised Vice-Admiral Jokic that we should meet on his ship with representatives of the Dubrovnik Crisis Committee later that day to commence these negotiations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that you had been told that General Ruzinovski was the commander. Had you ever been told about Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Admiral Jokic volunteer to meet with you?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he comply with the general's order?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What branch of the service was General Ruzinovski?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What branch was Admiral Jokic in?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Navy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The liaison officer, the Captain Jeremic, what branch of the service was he in?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: He was navy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After these appointments or assignments were made, did anything else occur at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: The general expressed the fact that he -- there was no intention of continuing on any attacks and that a cease-fire would be maintained around Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any discussion about any upcoming meetings?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: The upcoming meetings were discussed in respect of General Jokic's meeting on board his ship, that that should take place immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who stated that the meeting should take place immediately?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: General Ruzinovski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Admiral Jokic comply with that?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the meeting end shortly after that or did it go on for a while?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: The meeting ended shortly after that so that we could return to Dubrovnik, pick up the Crisis Committee, and return to the Bay of Kotor to meet with Admiral Jokic on his ship.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What did you do? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: After that, we returned to Dubrovnik. We picked up the Crisis Committee, namely the mayor of Dubrovnik, the president of the Assembly of Dubrovnik, an engineer because of the requirement to get agreement for the repair of electricity and water supplies, plus, of course, our interpreter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do once you met with these representatives from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: We got on our little boat again and went down to the Bay of Kotor about 3.00 in the afternoon and boarded the vessel on which Admiral Jokic was located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else from the JNA was on that vessel?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: The Captain Svicevic, if I can pronounce his name correctly. I do apologise about this. He was one of the officers who was at the previous meeting. Captain Jeremic Sofronije, our liaison officer, and there were some other officers in attendance as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let me get this straight: In this meeting were the JNA representatives?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The local representatives from Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who from your team?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: The same members that went to meet with General Ruzinovski; Mr. Nolan, Mr. Zak, and myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did someone chair or run this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Vice-Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you please tell us about the discussion that occurred at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: The discussion at that meeting centred initially on the need for the area around Komolac, where the electricity substation was located and which had been damaged, to be secured from further attacks from the hills surrounding it, and for agreement to be obtained from the JNA that repair work to the electricity supply and water supply in the area could commence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was there a need for security for the workers to commence the work?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Because a number of Croatian workers had been killed earlier in that area of the water supply line and electricity substation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How had they been killed?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: It was alleged that they had been killed by JNA sniper fire from the hills surrounding that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Admiral Jokic respond to the requests?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He agreed that the area would be secured as quickly as possible and that thereafter repair work could be undertaken by the Croatians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say how long it would be before the work could begin?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I can't recall whether there was a specific time frame for this, but it was certainly a very short one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did this meeting last?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: The meeting lasted about a couple of hours, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would you describe the atmosphere?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: The atmosphere was, I would say, professional, as was our previous meeting with General Ruzinovski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any discussion made concerning any future meetings?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was agreed that there should be daily meetings between the team and the JNA and also that the Crisis Committee would attend some of these meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any other meetings on that date?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Not on that date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you maintain a diary in relation to the meetings on that date and others?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you place in the diary?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I placed a record of the -- of all the happenings of that day, in respect of our meetings between the JNA and the Dubrovnik Crisis Committee. It was a fairly detailed summary of what transpired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you prepare this? Did you do it by yourself, with others?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: This was prepared from notes we had taken at the actual meetings themselves. It was prepared at our hotel that evening, between the three of us. I actually acted as the scribe for this -- for the note-taking purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "the three of us," you're talking about the --

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the three ECMM members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you prepare this diary at the end of each day?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, we would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the information still fresh in your minds?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was. And it was information which we conveyed to Zagreb whenever possible through our car radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now the ECMM, do they maintain any sort of reporting structure?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. There was a daily reporting structure for all teams to report at the end of their task for the day. They would report to the tasking cell, and each day there would be a meeting of the heads of the various delegations which made up the ECMM in Zagreb, chaired by the ambassador, so that reports of any significance could be forwarded to the Presidency at The Hague. And it would also -- it would also determine any future operational requirements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was the reason that you maintained a daily diary, was that to provide notes to the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were those notes in fact provided to the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And having worked in the tasking cell, what happens when notes are sent forward?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, when notes are sent forward, they are maintained in the normal course of events in the ECMM filing system and, if necessary, provided for the benefit of the heads of delegations' daily meetings with the ambassador.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these notes filed and kept and maintained in the ordinary course of government business, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, they are, in the -- in the normal circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We'll get back to the records a little later, but let's move on to the next day, October 12, 1991. Could you tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: We had made arrangements to meet with the JNA side at a place just outside Cavtat on the borders of the airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do you get to Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: We got to Cavtat by motor vessel because it was again considered too dangerous to travel there by car at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so where did you meet this vessel? Was this another ferry or --

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: No. This was -- this varied, in fact, from occasion to occasion. It was either a little fishing vessel or a small motor boat that had been loaned by a local resident for this purpose, and we would then go to Cavtat. At Cavtat, we would then board a white minibus, again provided by the local authority at Cavtat, and drive to a pre-agreed rendezvous, where we would be met by the JNA liaison officer, Captain Jeremic Sofronije.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did this trip take going from Dubrovnik to arrival at the JNA liaison point in Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: About a couple of hours. About a couple of hours, I would say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how were you dressed, by the way? Were you dressed in a uniform of some kind?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: No, not a uniform. We were dressed in white as best as may be; white cricket trousers for myself with a white jumper and a borrowed white Italian army camouflage smock to keep us dry if it rained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you wear this set of clothing on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you armed?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at the meeting point at Cavtat on that date, did anything happen?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: We arrived -- if my memory is correct, we arrived at the rendezvous point and were met by a captain of the JNA navy, if I'm getting my dates right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're referring to October 12th.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard the name Captain Zec?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, I have. We were met by this Captain Zec. Did I say Zak before? I meant Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may interrupt just for a second to say something that I would not like to become our practice, and I hope you will share my opinion. The witness has come before the Honourable Court to tell what he best remembers and what he knows. With all due respect to the witness and to our learned friends, if the witness is unable to remember something, I don't think it is appropriate for the Prosecutor to suggest the name of the person he had met with or to refresh his memory in the examination-in-chief in any way, because, at least in my understanding, it is not acceptable. Therefore, I would grateful to my colleague to simply ask the question, see if the witness remembers, or maybe does not remember, and leave it at that. I did not react the first time this happened, but I would really like this not to become the practice in this case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I don't think you really need me to develop further what has been put by Mr. Petrovic. You did lead on that matter quite obviously, and I can rely on you, I'm sure, to be more careful in future.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would just like to state that I was trying to save a little time in refreshing recollection, which is authorised through the Appeals Court of this -- of the ICTY. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us continue. Now, you met with this captain. Of what branch of the service did he belong?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Navy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you what his position was?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: He was acting on behalf of the Admiral Jokic at the time, also of General Ruzinovski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he with anyone?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: He was with the liaison officer and surrounded, in fact, by JNA forces, all armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have any conversation with the captain?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We were surprised to meet him in such circumstances, because it was in fact quite intimidating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "such circumstances," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: To be surrounded by armed JNA forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in a building?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: No, we weren't. This was before we got to any building. It was at the rendezvous point where we met the liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there any conversation?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, there was. He advised us that there had been an attack on JNA forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and for that reason, because some soldiers of the JNA had been killed, meeting would have to be -- that had been arranged for that day would have to be postponed by 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he give you anything?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: He gave us a letter from General Ruzinovski explaining the position and saying that the meeting would have to be postponed for 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to show you a letter. Would you look on the monitor, please. It's letter that has a number on the top, 02191320. That's on the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think if you could give the number again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. In the English, the number is 02191320. In the B/C/S version --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't read it. Yes, I see this letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you read the letter or --

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Ah, that's better. Yes, I can read the letter now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you recognise it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I recognise it because I had that in my possession, and I think I initialed it at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do with the letter?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I kept the letter and eventually handed it in to the tasking cell at Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you maintain a copy for yourself or --

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, I did, kept it secure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I ask you to look to the bottom, say, three-quarters of the way down the page to the right. There is some --

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: That's my initials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And, sir, has this document been changed or altered since you've last seen it?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: No, it hasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to tender this document as well as the B/C/S version of the same.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document will be numbered Prosecution Exhibit P1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. That may be a convenient time then, Mr. Weiner, for the break. We will at this time, Mr. Stringer, have a break to enable, firstly, tapes to be changed; secondly, to enable Mr. Strugar and I believe yourself to move around a little and have a rest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume in quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, let us continue. We're outside of Cavtat on October 12th, and you were handed a letter by Captain Zec from General Ruzinovski.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if anything else, happened?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Captain Zec also handed a letter to the mayor of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you able to learn what that letter was?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: The letter contained a number of conditions which were required to be met by the authorities in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know who authored the letter or signed the letter?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: It was signed on or on behalf of Vice-Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was there any discussion with you in relation to that letter?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Not specifically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given that same letter?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: What happened next was that we had a brief discussion with Captain Zec, who said that General Ruzinovski had agreed that the repairs to the electricity and water supply should proceed and that there should be a meeting continuing next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any further discussion?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Only to express our concerns about the events, which we did not feel merited a delay in having the meetings with the -- between the JNA and the Dubrovnik Crisis Committee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any statements made by Captain Zec?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I can't recall precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that you had -- you maintained a diary.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does your diary discuss the happenings and the meetings of 12 October 1991?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would like to show him a page from his diary to see if it refreshes his recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Actually, page 7 of the statement, which is the typed version.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you will bear with me, I would only like clarification at this point. I hope I will not take up too much of my learned friend's time. I did not understand whether the witness will be shown his own written statement that he had given to an investigator of the Prosecution or some other document. If it concerns his written statement, then if I understand things correctly, that is unacceptable. And if it is another document, I would like to know which. But to refresh the witness's memory using his witness statement given to the investigator is not admissible, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understood, Mr. Petrovic, that it was to be an extract from his own diary, but if that's not the case, we will see.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. It is a copy of the extract from his diary. It is in his witness statement, but it is a copy of the extract. I can show him either one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it would be good to go away from the statement, Mr. Weiner. Mr. Petrovic's point is well made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I invite your attention to the last sentence -- actually, why don't you look at page 26. Could you read that to yourself, please -- I'm sorry, paragraph 26 from your diary.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having looked at your diary and read that, does that refresh your recollection as to the statement made by Captain Zec to you?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. This was made to us not in the presence of the Dubrovnik committee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Where he said that in our informal discussions that it was the intention of the JNA to complete their tactical successes and that they had to capability to do so if they wished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, was there any further conversation?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Only to the effect that Captain Zec confirmed that General Ruzinovski had said that the repairs to the electricity substation and water supply should proceed and that there should be a meeting continuing next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's go to the next day. Did they in fact hold a meeting?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: At a location just on the border of the airport, outside Cavtat. I think the name of the location was Zvekovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who was present on this -- at this meeting of October 13th, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, at the Croatian side there was the deputy mayor, a member of the Dubrovnik Assembly, and the engineer from Dubrovnik. On the JNA side, there was Captain Svicevic, who had been present on the previous occasions; the liaison officer, Captain Jeremic Sofronije; and another lieutenant colonel of the JNA army. I think his name was Colonel Sulejman. I can't remember his final name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who chaired or ran this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Captain Svicevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was discussed at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought the earphones had gone. At that meeting, Captain Svicevic said that the area around Komolac, the electricity substation, had been secured and that repairs could be undertaken the following day. We also raised a number of other matters concerning the blockade of Dubrovnik and, in particular, the need for medical and food supplies to be allowed through. We also raised the question of refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you seen any refugees up to that point?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: We had seen refugees in the area of Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the discussion in relation to refugees?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: We wanted some assurance as to the refugees' well-being, but we were advised that the refugees should be moved out of Dubrovnik to the north and south.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any other discussion about Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Captain Svicevic made it quite clear that it was not the JNA's intention to attack Dubrovnik and stressed that they wanted Dubrovnik preserved for its historical and cultural importance to Yugoslavia as a whole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any other discussion relating to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: On that particular occasion, I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One moment, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in your diary, do you discuss your meetings of the 13th?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the end of the day, did you take any notes in relation to the 13th?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I recorded it in my notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. One moment. Sir, I'd like to direct your attention to paragraph 39 to see if that refreshes your recollection. Just read it to yourself first.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then also paragraph 40.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what other conversation was occurring at the time?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Conversation then rested on the change of command between General Ruzinovski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: We were advised by Svicevic that General Ruzinovski was changing command, and he handed us a letter to this effect from General Ruzinovski saying that General Strugar would be assuming command from him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to look at the screen and look at this letter. The ERN at the top should be 02191322 on the English translation and 01291321 on the B/C/S translation. Looking at the English translation, do you recognise this letter?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, I do. My initials are at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Through my initials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the content?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I recognise -- I recall the content of it now, because it was complimentary in tone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was that the letter that you received on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do with that letter?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I took it back with me to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do once you got to Zagreb with it?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: Then it was presented again to the tasking cell and eventually filed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you maintain a copy for yourself?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have any changes --

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: There have been no changes to that letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there have been no changes or alterations to it made since you've last seen it?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: None at all, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We would like to offer the English as well as the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be numbered Prosecution Exhibit P2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, as part of the discussion concerning this change in personnel, was there any discussion as to changes in scope of authority or --

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: I understood that the scope of authority remained the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, was there any discussion about Croatian forces on that date?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: There were accusations that Croatian forces were using the Old City of Dubrovnik as a, what I might say a hide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the response?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: We said that we had seen no Croatian forces within the Old City.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever seen anyone that was armed in the city?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER
utterances.text: We'd seen the local police in normal police uniforms who were lightly armed, but not military personnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What colour uniforms?
